mcqs.question: In the heap-based Dijkstra implementation, why does popping a node that's already in the finalized set simply skip it with continue, rather than an error?
options: Because the heap only allows each node to be pushed once, so this case can never actually happen
Because it indicates the graph has a negative edge weight
Because that pop represents a stale entry left over from an earlier, now-outdated relaxation, and the node's true shortest distance was already found the first time it was popped
Because it signals the algorithm has finished and should terminate
mcqs.explanation: Lazy deletion means the same node can be pushed multiple times as its tentative distance improves, leaving stale entries in the heap — the first pop of any node is guaranteed to carry its true shortest distance, so every later pop of that same node is outdated and safely skipped. This has nothing to do with negative weights or overall termination, and the heap absolutely can contain duplicate entries for the same node.

mcqs.question: The proof that Dijkstra's greedy choice is safe relies on which specific property of the graph's edge weights?
options: All edge weights are non-negative, so no later edge on a path can undercut an already-finalized shorter prefix
All edge weights are equal to each other
The graph must be a tree with no cycles
Every node must have the same number of outgoing edges
mcqs.explanation: Non-negative weights guarantee that extending a path can never decrease its total cost, which is exactly what rules out a supposedly-shortest prefix later being undercut by a path through a not-yet-finalized node. Equal weights would just make it a BFS special case, and neither tree structure nor uniform node degree has anything to do with the correctness argument.

mcqs.question: On a very dense graph where E is close to V^2, how does the plain-array version of Dijkstra's compare to the heap-based version?
options: The array version's O(V^2) can actually match or beat the heap version's O((V+E) log V), since the log factor stops paying off once E approaches V^2
The heap-based version is always faster regardless of graph density
The array version cannot correctly handle dense graphs at all
Both versions have identical complexity on any graph
mcqs.explanation: When E approaches V^2, the heap version's (V+E) term is dominated by E, making its complexity roughly V^2 log V — worse than the array version's flat O(V^2), since the log factor is pure overhead once the graph is dense enough. The array version handles dense graphs perfectly well, and the two are not identical in complexity across graph shapes.

mcqs.question: In 0-1 BFS, why is a neighbor reached via a 0-weight edge pushed to the FRONT of the deque, while a neighbor reached via a 1-weight edge is pushed to the back?
options: Front-pushing is just an arbitrary implementation convention with no effect on correctness
It has no bearing on distance ordering — it only affects which node happens to be processed first among ties

A 0-weight edge doesn't increase distance at all, so that neighbor is equally close to the current node and belongs at the same priority level, while a 1-weight edge genuinely adds one unit of distance
Front-pushing is required to prevent the deque from growing unbounded
mcqs.explanation: The front/back placement directly encodes distance without needing a heap's comparison logic: a 0-weight edge means no distance increase, so that neighbor belongs at the same priority as the current node (front), while a 1-weight edge genuinely adds a unit of distance and belongs one level further out (back). This is a deliberate correctness mechanism, not an arbitrary convention, a tie-breaking detail, or a memory-bound concern.

mcqs.question: You run standard Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph that happens to contain one negative-weight edge. What actually happens?
options: The algorithm throws a clear error indicating negative weights are not supported
It silently completes and may return an incorrect shortest-distance value, since the greedy-safety proof no longer holds
It automatically switches to Bellman-Ford internally to handle the negative edge
It correctly computes the answer, just more slowly than usual
mcqs.explanation: Dijkstra has no built-in check for negative weights — it runs to completion and can finalize a node before a cheaper path through the negative edge is discovered, silently producing a wrong distance with no error or slowdown to signal the problem. There's no automatic fallback to another algorithm; using a graph that might have negative weights safely requires switching to Bellman-Ford deliberately.

mcqs.question: An implementation of Dijkstra's algorithm omits the check for whether a popped node is already finalized. What's the practical consequence?
options: The algorithm wastes work re-processing a node's neighbors using an already-outdated, worse distance value, and in a variant that also updates dist[node] on re-pop, results can be actively corrupted
The algorithm crashes with an index-out-of-range error
This has no observable effect under any circumstances
The heap will grow without bound and eventually run out of memory
mcqs.explanation: Without the finalized check, a stale heap entry that's popped a second time can trigger redundant relaxation using an outdated distance — wasted work at minimum, and in implementations that don't carefully guard the distance-update step, this can actively corrupt the result. It won't crash on its own, isn't a complete no-op, and doesn't by itself cause unbounded heap growth — the heap size is still bounded by the number of relaxations performed.
